'''''Trachelospermum asiaticum''''', the '''Asiatic jasmine''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Apocynaceae]] and it is [[native species|native]] to Asia.<ref name="Plants of the World Online">{{cite web |title=''Trachelospermum asiaticum'' (Siebold & Zucc.) Nakai |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:82528-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Kew Science |accessdate=17 June 2020}}</ref> Its flowers resemble stars, so it is also referred to as '''yellow star jasmine''' or '''Asian star jasmine'''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trachelospermum asiaticum (Asian Star Jasmine, Asiatic Jasmine, Yellow Star Jasmine) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/trachelospermum-asiaticum/|access-date=2021-12-08|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> This is a fast growing evergreen vine, often used to cover fences, walls, and similar surfaces. It is heat- and cold- tolerant, and grows even in shady areas.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-07-15|title=How to grow and trim Asiatic jasmine|url=https://shinyplant.com/grow-asiatic-jasmine/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210121225306/https://shinyplant.com/grow-asiatic-jasmine/|url-status=usurped|archive-date=January 21, 2021|access-date=2021-02-10|website=Shiny Plant|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The Latin [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''asiaticum'' means "from Asia".

It was first described by [[Philipp Franz von Siebold]] and [[Joseph Gerhard Zuccarini]] in 1846. [[Bavarians|Bavarian]] physician and naturalist Siebold spent time in Japan between 1823 and 1829. Back in Germany with his collections, he was assisted by Zuccarini, professor of botany at [[LMU Munich]] to describe this plant under its original name of ''Malouetia asiatica'' (1846).

==Description==
Growing to {{convert|6|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall, ''Trachelospermum asiaticum'' is a woody, [[evergreen]] [[vine|climber]] with glossy, leathery leaves and strongly scented cream-coloured flowers in summer.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref> The stems, when cut, exude a milky white latex. The leaves are simple and opposite, persistent, borne by a [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] 2–10 mm, with an elliptic limb, narrowly ovate, 2–10 x 1–5 cm, membranous. Glossy green leaves have a brown-orange tinge stained reddish during the winter. The [[Hardiness (plants)|hardiest]] ''Trachelospermum'' species, this plant can be grown in [[temperateness|temperate]] areas against a sheltered wall or fence. It has been known to spread rapidly, and can take over large areas very rapidly.<ref>Mori Tamezô, An Enumeration of Plants Hitherto Known From Corea 293. 1922</ref>

===Inflorescence=== 
The white or cream flowers have a yellow heart and emit a scent of [[jasmine]]. They are held in terminal or axillary [[cymes]]. The five [[sepals]] are contiguous to the tube of the [[corolla (botany)|corolla]] and carry 10 basal glands. The [[hypocrateriform]] corolla consists of a tube 6-10mm long, with an enlarged throat, and five [[obovate]] lobes, as long as the tube. The [[stamen]]s are inserted into the throat of the corolla tube. The [[anther]]s are exerted (protrude outside the tube, unlike T. jasminoides). The hairless [[ovary]] consists of two [[carpel]]s. Flowering takes place from late spring to summer.

The fruit consists of two linear [[Follicle (fruit)|follicle]]s, 10–30 by 0.3–0.5 cm. The seeds are oblong with at one end a 3.5 cm [[egret]].<ref>Fumiko A and Tatsuo Y, "  Glycosides of 19α-Hydroxyoleanan-type triterpenoids from Trachelospermum asiaticum (Trachelospermum IV)  ", Chem Pharm Bull, vol.  35, n o  5,1987</ref>

==Range==
[[File:Trachelospermum_asiaticum_cv2.jpg|thumb|200px|Variegated variety]]
[[File:Trachelospermum_jasminoides-asiaticum.jpg|thumb|200px|Comparison of ''T. jasminoides'' and ''T. asiaticum'']]
''Trachelospermum asiaticum'' is native to China, [[India]], Japan, [[Korea]], [[Indo-China]] and [[Malaysia]]. It grows in [[montane forest|mountain forest]]s and [[Shrubland|scrub]], often attached to trees.

==Cultivation==
Quite similar to the false jasmine ''[[Trachelospermum jasminoides]]'', ''T. asiaticum'' produces flowers with a slightly smaller yellow or cream heart. It has faster growth in the early years. It provides an evergreen ornamental ground cover, or, as a liana, planted along a wall or trellis, in semi-shade or sunny exposure, providing intense fragrance during the flowering period in summer. It can withstand brief frosts down to -15 °C.<ref>Christophe Wiart, Ethnopharmacology of medicinal plants Asia and the Pacific, Totowa, NJ, Humana Press, 2006 ( {{ISBN|1588297489}}, 9781588297488, 9781597451604 and 1597451606</ref>

It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Trachelospermum asiaticum'' | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/18282/Trachelospermum-asiaticum/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>

There are several cultivars with various patterns of variegation and also dwarf varieties.

==Chemical composition== 
Many [[flavonoid]]s were extracted from the leaves of ''Trachelospermum asiaticum'' var. ''intermedium'': [[apigenin]] 7-Oglucoside, [[luteolin]], [[luteolin]]-4, [[rhoifolin]], lonicerine, [[kaempferol]] 3-O-[[rhamnoside]], [[quercitrin]], and [[phenol]]ic compounds such as [[lignan]] and chlorogenic acid.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hosoi |first1=Shinzo |last2=Shimizu |first2=Eri |last3=Tanaka |first3=Toshihiro |last4=Sakai |first4=Eiji |last5=Yamada |first5=Mitsuko |last6=Sakushima |first6=Akiyo |title=Main phenolic compounds from the flower of ''Trachelospermum asiaticum'' var. ''intermedium'' (Apocynaceae) |journal=Journal of Natural Medicines |date=2008 |volume=62 |issue=3 |pages=354–355 |doi=10.1007/s11418-008-0232-5}}</ref>

Of [[triterpene]]s oleanolic type were also detected: the acid 2α, 3β, 19α, 23,24-pentahydroxyoléan-12-en-28-oic acid or trachélospérogénine E 8.
